sections.body:
Dating language is the set of words people use to describe what is happening between them, and to decide how much it means. It is a working vocabulary, not a rulebook. Two people can use the same word and mean different things, which is why almost every confusion in dating comes down to one question: what did each of us think this was?

The vocabulary has moved fast because the behaviour moved fast. Dating moved from a phone call to a message, from fixed plans to vague availability, from a small circle to a whole city. Each change brought new words and left old ones behind, sometimes with new meanings. A word like 'date' once implied a plan made in advance. Today it can be one message and a coffee, or it can be a whole relationship that neither person has named.

The useful way to read this vocabulary is not to memorise definitions but to ask three questions about any label. What behaviour does it describe? What expectations does it carry? And what does it say about how the other person sees the situation? A label that answers those three things tells you more than any definition could.

This article gives you the labels and their real meanings, then the practical side: reading a profile, planning a first meeting, talking on a date, handling mixed signals, and ending something clearly. The examples are written so you can copy them.
examples: Sorry for the slow reply — I've been a bit buried this week.
Are we calling this a date, or are we just seeing how it goes?
sections.heading: What dating language actually means

sections.body:
These six words carry most of the meaning in modern dating. Learn them and most conversations become much easier to have, because you will be able to say what you think is happening.

A **crush** is an intense feeling for someone you have not got close to. A **date** is a planned meeting with someone you are getting to know, with the expectation of spending time together. A **situationship** is a relationship without a label, where nobody has said what it is. **Ghosting** is disappearing without explanation. **Breadcrumbing** is keeping someone interested with occasional contact and no intention of meeting. An **ex** is someone you have been in a relationship with and are no longer in one.

Two of these are about the other person's behaviour rather than about the relationship: ghosting and breadcrumbing. They are worth recognising early, because both cost time and both are easier to act on before you have invested much.
sections.heading: The labels people use, one by one

terms.example: I have a crush on someone from my office, but we have only ever said hello.
terms.gloss: An intense feeling of attraction for someone you have not yet got close to.

terms.example: Is Friday a date, or just a coffee between friends?
terms.gloss: A planned meeting with someone you are getting to know. It implies time set aside for each other.

terms.example: We have been seeing each other for months and calling it a situationship.
terms.gloss: A relationship that has no agreed label. Nobody has said what it is, and nobody has asked.

terms.example: He replied for three weeks and then ghosted me completely.
terms.gloss: Stopping all contact without explanation, so the other person is left waiting and guessing.

terms.example: He messages me every few days but has never once suggested meeting.
terms.gloss: Sending occasional messages to keep someone interested while never making any real plan.

terms.example: My ex and I still share a group of friends, so we keep it simple.
terms.gloss: Someone you were in a relationship with and are no longer in one.

sections.body:
The definitions are easy; the practice is where labels mislead. Here is what each one tends to look like in real life.

A **crush** involves feelings and very little information. The risk is treating a crush as a relationship that already exists, because one side is usually doing far more thinking than the other.

A **date** is a meeting with an expectation. If one person treats it as a date and the other treats it as a favour to a friend, both will leave confused. Say which one you think it is. 'This was a date for me — I enjoyed it, and I'd like to do it again' costs one sentence and removes the whole problem.

A **situationship** is not a failure state. It is a mutual agreement to keep the labels off, usually because neither wants to define things yet. It becomes a problem only when one person is using it to avoid a conversation the other is waiting for.

Ghosting is a choice, and it is usually made to avoid an uncomfortable message. What it actually communicates is only the choice to avoid. **Breadcrumbing** is different: it is a habit of keeping options open. The pattern to watch is not a single slow reply; it is regular contact with no plan ever made.

And an **ex** is a category of person, not a category of feeling. Most exes are fine; a few are not; and the difference is usually about how the relationship ended, not about the person.
examples: This was a date for me — I had a good time, and I'd like to do it again.
We're both happy to keep it casual — I just wanted to check we were on the same page.
sections.heading: What each label means in practice

sections.body:
A profile is a shop window, and a first message is a shop assistant. Both are advertisements, and both are edited to produce one specific effect: a reply.

Read the profile for what is actually offered rather than what is claimed. The photos tell you about style and about how many attempts at a photo there were, which says something about effort. The bio tells you about tone: a joke-heavy bio wants banter, a straight bio wants straightness. The 'looking for' section is the only part that says what the person actually wants, and it is usually the most carefully written part.

Then read the first message. A message that names something specific from the profile — a photo, a line, a detail — was written for you. A message that could be sent to anyone was sent to many people. The difference is worth noticing, because your reply quality depends on it.

And check the effort in the message. A typo or two is normal. A message with no question, no detail and no hint of reading the profile usually means the reply you send will be treated the same way. If you want the conversation to go somewhere, you will have to supply the first real detail yourself.
examples: Your photo at the museum made me curious — have you been there recently?
The photo with the dog is good. How long have you had him?
sections.heading: How to read a profile and a first message

sections.body:
A first date is mostly a test of one thing: can we be comfortable together for an hour and a half. That is why so much advice about first dates is about logistics rather than conversation.

On the words themselves, three habits work well. First, ask questions that have stories in them: how did you end up doing this, what is the best thing that happened to you this year. Avoid questions that can be answered with a job title or a one-word answer.

Second, use the pause. A little silence after someone finishes is not a failure of the conversation; it is the space where they decide to say the interesting part instead of the safe part. Filling every gap yourself is the main reason some conversations feel empty.

Third, put something of your own on the table early. Not a résumé — a small, real thing: a piece of news, a trip that went wrong, a habit you have. Reciprocity is what makes a first date feel like two people rather than an interview.

And notice what the other person does with time. Someone who checks their phone the whole time, answers in one word, or is in a hurry to leave is telling you something. You do not need to decode it on the spot; you only need to notice.
examples: What made you end up in this line of work?
What's the best thing that happened to you this year?
I'll tell you a story about the last flight I took, but it's a bad one.
sections.heading: The words people use on a first date

sections.body:
A good first meeting is easy to arrange, cheap to cancel, and public. That sounds like dull advice, but it solves most of the problems people have with first dates.

Plan something with a natural end, in a public place, where a conversation can happen but you are not trapped. A coffee, a short walk, a market, a bookshop with chairs. If you are meeting someone for the first time, do not choose a place where you cannot leave without making a scene.

Propose a specific time and a specific place. 'Sometime this week' produces a week of silence. 'Saturday at 4 at the café on the corner' produces a plan, and a plan can be confirmed, moved, or cancelled clearly.

Then, if it goes well, say so before you part, and propose the next one. Most dating goes wrong not at the first meeting but in the gap after it, where nobody makes the second plan.
examples: Would Saturday at 4 at the café on the corner work for you?
I have to head off at six, but I really enjoyed this — can we do it again next week?
sections.heading: How to plan a first meeting
steps: Choose somewhere public, casual and easy to leave.
Propose a specific day and time, not 'sometime soon'.
Keep it short: about ninety minutes is plenty for a first meeting.
Tell the other person what you have in mind so they can prepare.
If it goes well, make the next plan before you leave.

sections.body:
Mixed signals happen for ordinary reasons. Someone is shy, busy, unsure, or has just come out of something that hurt. The problem is not the signals; it is the guessing. Guessing consumes enormous energy, and it produces the worst conversations at the worst moment.

So ask. Directly, kindly, and once. The point of a direct question is not to force an answer but to remove the noise around it. 'Are you seeing other people?' and 'What are you looking for?' are uncomfortable for about ten seconds and then save weeks.

Ask about behaviour rather than about feelings when you can, because behaviour is easier to answer honestly. 'Do you want to see me again?' is answerable. 'Do you care about me?' is not, because nobody agrees on what it means.

If the other person will not answer, treat that as an answer. Someone who cannot say 'I'm not sure yet' or 'I'm seeing someone else' is telling you that they do not want to be clear, and you are allowed to stop waiting. Being unclear is a choice, and it is a choice you do not have to wait for.

And if you are the one being unclear because you are enjoying the attention, remember that the longer you stay vague, the more expensive the eventual honesty becomes.
examples: Are you seeing other people at the moment?
I'd like to understand where we stand — is this a dating thing for you?
Would you like to meet again this week, or would you rather leave it here?
sections.heading: Mixed signals and how to ask about them

terms.example: He texts every day but has cancelled three plans — those are mixed signals.
terms.gloss: When one person's behaviour and words point in different directions, usually because they are unsure or unwilling to say where things stand.

sections.body:
Dating customs differ widely, and most mistakes are not rudeness — they are translation errors. In some cultures, meeting someone's family early is a serious step. In others, not inviting a partner to a family meal is a sign of something. A text message may be warm in one country and intrusive in another.

The rule that helps in every case is to be explicit about what a given action means to you, rather than assuming the other person reads it the same way. 'I would like to introduce you to my parents' carries more information than the invitation itself, and it protects both of you from a wrong guess.

Language matters too. Where you share a first language, small ambiguities are usually fine. Where you do not, be more literal and more patient. Write down a date or a time rather than relying on 'tomorrow' or 'next week'. Ask for a name spelling at the start, because a misspelled name is a small thing that colours a whole relationship.

And when in doubt about a custom, ask. 'Is it normal to meet the family at this stage?' is a better question than a silent assumption.
examples: When we have been seeing each other for a while, I would like to introduce you to my family.
Let me check my calendar — what day works best for you?
sections.heading: Dating across cultures and languages

sections.body:
Most dating pain comes from wanting different things and neither person saying so. The remedy is uncomfortable for about one conversation and then permanent.

Say what you want early, in plain words, and then let the other person answer honestly. Say what you are looking for: a relationship, something casual, company for weekends, or you do not know yet. Say what you are not willing to do. Say what you need from someone who is close to you: messages, time, honesty about who else is in the picture.

Two practical points. First, honesty is not the same as pressure: 'I would like to see you more than once a week' is a statement; 'Why don't you text me more?' is an accusation. Second, ask about consent and intention directly in anything that matters, and treat a clear no as a complete answer that needs no follow-up.

People who state their wants plainly attract the people who actually want them. The ones who never say anything spend months hoping the right person guesses.
examples: I would like to see you more than once a week.
I'm not ready for a long relationship unless we're both sure.
sections.heading: Say what you want, early and plainly

terms.example: Consent has to be clear on both sides, and a no is always a complete answer.
terms.gloss: Everyone agreeing freely to something, every time. A clear no is a complete answer that needs no follow-up.

sections.body:
Every dating situation ends. Some end because a relationship has run its course, some because the other person disappeared, and some because you were the one who stopped wanting it. How you end it determines what people say about you afterwards and, more importantly, how you feel about it a month later.

Be brief, be kind, and be clear. The three sentences that do the job are: an acknowledgement of what was good, a statement that you do not want to continue, and a wish for the other person. 'I've had a good time with you, but I don't think I want to keep dating, and I wish you all the best.' That is enough. Anything more invites a negotiation you have already finished in your own head.

Do not leave the other person to work it out. A slow fade is the cruelest ending available, because it forces someone else to spend weeks forming and discarding hope. If you are not going to see someone again, send the message.

And when you are the one being ended, let it be. Ask one question if the answer matters, but do not negotiate for a decision that has already been made. A clean ending is a kindness you can give yourself too: it closes the loop, and it lets you move on without the background hum of an unfinished story.
examples: I've really enjoyed meeting you, but I don't think this is going anywhere, and I wish you well.
I don't think we should keep meeting, but I wanted to tell you myself rather than let it fade.
Thank you for a lovely evening. I hope things go well for you.
sections.heading: Ending it well

item.summary: Dating has a vocabulary of its own: a crush, a date, a situationship, ghosting, breadcrumbing. After reading this you know what each label means in practice, how to read a profile and a first message, what to say on a first date, how to ask about mixed signals, and how to end something without hurting anyone.
item.title: Understanding Modern Dating Expressions
